column3: Direct parallel: the claim is rejected through divine self-sufficiency, ownership, and lack of warrant.
Speech etiquette does not clarify the claim, ownership, or universal obedience in 2:116.
Nearly repeats the possession and universal qanitun conclusion, confirming all creatures stand under God.
Recasts the alleged offspring as honored servants, sharply distinguishing service from divine descent.
Its competing communal assertions and final judgment only loosely frame disputed religious speech.
Contrasts seeking honor through others with honor belonging wholly to God; the relation is indirect.
Directly identifies the child claim as the object of warning, though it adds little beyond that.
The dispute over receiving good from the Lord does not materially illuminate 2:116.
Rejects independently taken protectors, a secondary contrast to assigning relationships alongside God.
Restates the claim about the Most Merciful, retaining its accusatory formulation but adding little.
Links ignorant demand-making to recurrent speech, only indirectly relevant to an unsupported attribution.
Joins denial of child, partner, and needful protector, defining divine greatness as independence.
Connects transcendence from offspring with the One, Overpowering God; it is a compressed parallel.
Divine power over every thing indirectly supports the immediate context but does not address offspring.
Gives a human instance of qanitun, illustrating obedient creaturehood without the polemical claim.
Explicitly combines no child, no partner in dominion, and measured creation.
The immediate continuation grounds the claim in origination of heaven and earth by decisive command.
Reinforces universal dominion and power, but largely repeats the ownership premise already established.
Denies child and co-deity, then supplies a contrary model of divided creation and rivalry.
Its ownership of heaven and earth and absence of protector reinforce the local premise indirectly.
Explicitly denies both consort and child, expanding the rejected familial frame.
The challenge over creating heaven and earth supports the creator-creature distinction behind 2:116.
The demand for proof is a general check on assertions, with no specific offspring content.
Directly rejects invented sons and daughters and marks the attribution as made without knowledge.
New creation may imply creative power, but it does not clarify the child claim.
The warning about questioning the messenger is not an interpretive addition to 2:116.
Labels the assertion that God begot as false, but contributes only a concise repetition.
Corrects exaggerated claims about the Messiah through one God, comprehensive ownership, and no child.
Religious-group pressure and guidance are too indirect despite the nearby context.
Human parenthood supplies only a lexical contrast, not an explanation of divine transcendence.
Cosmic scope and transcendence from association reinforce immeasurable divine authority.
The closing affirmation of power is contextual but does not address the claim itself.
The oath by the constructed heaven adds no clear relation beyond a broad creation motif.
Universal tasbih supplies a fuller counterpart to universal qanitun: all creatures honor God in their modes.
Prayer, alms, and recompense do not materially explain 2:116.
Ibrahim as qanit to God supplies a human contrast to associating creaturely status with divinity.
Counters identifying God with the Messiah by stressing his vulnerability, God's creation, dominion, and power.
Submission to God loosely echoes qanitun but adds no explanation of the disputed attribution.
Universal tasbih overlaps the closing theme but is redundant and lacks the child claim.
Human qanitin illustrates obedience but is a narrow, repetitive parallel.
Blocking God's remembrance is only tangential to the statement of universal belonging.
The denunciation of slanderers does not clarify 2:116.
A claim about sealed hearts has only a remote connection through the verb of saying.
God's ownership of east and west broadens the local scope of all-encompassing divine presence and knowledge.
The concise denial of begetting and being begotten is a foundational parallel, though it is terse.
The contentious comparison of deities does not add a usable explanation here.
Taking a prescribed share of servants is not a clear interpretive link to 2:116.
A human example of qanut and reward is only a distant illustration of obedience.
The heaven-earth warning supplies authority imagery but no direct relation to offspring or ownership.
Adds that all in heaven and earth belong to God and that enduring devotion is due to Him.
Extended prostration and tasbih echo devotion without clarifying the central attribution.
Those with God are not too proud for worship, reinforcing the servant contrast in 21:26.
The reaction of opponents to fortune or misfortune has no material link.
Universal dominion and divine witness reinforce the comprehensive ownership premise, redundantly.
Sole lordship over east and west and taking God as trustee extend the exclusive-authority reading.
Directly argues from unique origination, lack of consort, creation of all things, and total knowledge.
Transcendence above associations is relevant but offers no further account of child attribution.
All intercession and dominion belong to God, limiting any imagined independent mediating share.
Mocking signs does not explain the semantic claims of 2:116.
God's knowledge of all heaven and earth indirectly challenges presumptuous claims made about Him.
Rejects unauthorized intercessory claims and joins this to transcendence from association.
All in heaven and earth continually ask of Him, adding creaturely dependence to universal belonging.
The oath by those who swim does not yield a clear addition.
Universal tasbih repeats the cosmic response already represented by stronger earlier parallels.
Heaven-earth authority is secondary and does not address descent or divine ownership directly enough.
The request to delay Moses and gather people is unrelated.
Exalting the highest Lord is a general transcendent frame, now highly redundant.
Combines universal tasbih, dominion, praise, and power, but reiterates established themes.
The catalogue of obedient men and women only distantly illustrates creaturely qanitun.
Explicitly denies taking a child and relates creation directly to the command 'Be.'
The messenger's wage and divine witness do not illuminate 2:116.
The ark's journey in God's name has no material interpretive link.
Directly rejects attributing daughters to God, adding a specific gendered form of the false attribution.
Universal tasbih is a redundant parallel to the closing universal obedience.
Cosmic administration suggests authority but does not clarify the claim or its rebuttal.
Creator, maker, former, and universal tasbih reinforce a creator-centered reading, with substantial overlap.
A group's declaration of tasbih is too narrow and repetitive to add much.
Universal dominion joined to giving life and death reinforces total divine power over creatures.
Lordship of heaven, earth, and what lies between is a broad but redundant scope statement.
Exclusive knowledge of the unseen, no protector besides Him, and no partner in judgment strongly exclude shared authority.
The list of favored prophets does not clarify divine offspring or universal ownership.
The Originator who feeds and is not fed provides a dependent-creature contrast to divine self-sufficiency.
Transcendence from association frames the issue generally but adds no specific support.
Reflection on creation and tasbih provides only a general cosmic-piety echo.
Dominion over every thing and return to God reinforce comprehensive possession, but repeat earlier evidence.
The Creator of every thing, sole God, and Overpowering One rules out powerless protectors and rival creators.
Military preparedness has no material connection.
Dominion over heaven and earth, judgment, forgiveness, and power reinforce unrestricted divine rule.
Regret over taking a friend is not a clear interpretive contribution.
Divine life, self-subsistence, ownership, knowledge, controlled intercession, and untiring preservation give a comprehensive parallel.
All in heaven and earth are subject to the final trumpet, a distant confirmation of universal creaturehood.
No escape in earth or heaven and no protector besides God only indirectly reinforce exclusivity.
The call to understand through hearts and ears does not add to 2:116.
The heaven with constellations is too generic to contribute.
Rejecting false authorities and holding to faith is a remote, non-specific contrast.
A claim about the unseen or covenant does not illuminate the child attribution.
Collective punishment and mutual blame are unrelated.
Provision in heaven does not clarify the semantic structure of 2:116.
God's self-sufficiency and human need sharpen the al-Ghani premise of the leading parallel.
Changing a commanded word and ensuing punishment are unrelated.
Jesus is compared with Adam, whose creation came by divine command rather than descent.
A human recipient of revelation does not direct people to worship him alongside God.
The claim that God is the Messiah is set against the Messiah's creaturely vulnerability.
The rejection of three directly reinforces one God against divided divinity.
The Messiah and his mother are shown as mortal servants who ate food, not divine offspring.
Jesus disavows calling people to take him and his mother as gods besides God.
God as Creator of every thing and sole object of worship extends the argument of 6:101.
Names specific claims that Ezra or the Messiah is God's son and identifies them as imitative speech.
Taking religious authorities as lords contrasts with worship of the one God.
Exposes the practice of assigning to God what people themselves dislike, clarifying 16:57.
Directly denies knowledge or warrant for the claim that God has taken a child.
Jesus identifies himself as God's servant, strengthening the servant rather than son contrast.
Jesus calls God his Lord and theirs, preserving the shared creature-to-Lord relation.
Treats the attribution to the Most Merciful as an immense and grave assertion.
The heavens, earth, and mountains are portrayed as recoiling from the child claim.
Restates the attribution to the Most Merciful within its climactic rebuttal.
Directly states that taking a child is unfitting for the Most Merciful.
Every being in heaven and earth comes to the Most Merciful as a servant.
God's complete enumeration of all beings reinforces comprehensive ownership and knowledge.
Each creature returns to Him individually, excluding familial co-divinity.
The honored servants act only by His command, further distinguishing them from offspring.
Their knowledge and intercession remain wholly bounded by His knowledge and permission.
A servant's claim to divinity besides God is explicitly subject to judgment.
The Creator of heaven and earth is able to create their like, reinforcing creative sufficiency.
When He wills a thing, His command is only 'Be,' directly paralleling 2:117.
Challenges the allocation of daughters to the Lord while reserving sons for the claimants.
Directly questions the alleged preference for daughters over sons in the false attribution.
God's creation of every thing and trusteeship over all reinforce universal possession.
Dominion over heaven and earth includes granting daughters and sons as created gifts.
Assigning a part of God's servants to Him directly conflicts with the servant status of creatures.
Directly challenges the claim that God took daughters while granting sons to people.
The naming of angels as daughters is rejected as an unwarranted attribution.
The Messiah is described as a servant favored by God, not a divine counterpart.
The conditional statement about a son preserves worship of the Most Merciful while refusing the premise.
Questions the unequal allocation of males to claimants and females to God.
Calls that allocation unjust, sharpening the critique of gendered divine attribution.
The declaration that God is One supplies the concise theological premise for rejecting divine offspring.
God's absolute self-sufficiency explains why no descendant or familial completion is needed.
